newsitem.title: UK: US rate rise unlikely to stir emerging mkts-Mobius.
newsitem.headline: US rate rise unlikely to stir emerging mkts-Mobius.

text.p: Templeton Emerging Markets President Mark Mobius, who has $9.0 billion in funds under management, said a small rise in the U.S. Fed funds following today's FOMC meeting was unlikely to startle emerging markets.
"I don't think emerging markets will be affected by any change in the short term unless it is very dramatic change which is not expected," Mobius told Reuters in an interview.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee meets later today and a 25 basis point rise in the Fed funds rate from the present 5.25 percent level is expected.
"It is only in times of very substantial change that you see the emerging markets react in one way or another," said Mobius.
"Mexico was an example where other markets in Latin America and even in Asia reacted...a lot of it is psychological reaction rather than one based on economic and financial facts."

He is also calm about the implications for Russian President Boris Yeltsin's ailing health on debt and equity markets. "Before the election everyone was concerned about whether Yeltsin would win and what would happen...we were not concerned because we thought the reforms that had taken place would stay."
"Even if Yeltsin's (heart) operation is not successful we would not be alarmed. There are enough good people to continue the reforms and to provide a stable system for the country."

He said a "halfway house" with an incapacitated president who has a successful operation but still needs a long time to recover" would stoke uncertainty. "But again it is mostly psychological. I think the market has discounted most of the fears of the operation."
Mobius said that amongst the three dozen emerging markets he regularly covers, he is raising weightings in Latin America.
"We are increasing the amounts we have in Latin America, although Hong Kong is still largest portion of our assets in emerging markets, followed by Brazil, Mexico and Argentina."

"Latin America is important because of the changes in government thinking there -- the reforms, the change from socialist thinking to market economy thinking, and the privatisation that follows from that."
"Our enthusiasm has not diminished even though the markets have come up substantially. There is lots of room to grow."
He said the recovery in Mexico was not complete and Brazil was finally embarking on its privatisation programme.

"Argentina is further along than Brazil and is now struggling with the transition from the orginal team which installed this new system. Now you have a new (government) team everyone is watching to see if it will continue."

In the emerging denbt market he said it would be difficult for Brady bonds to go much higher. "In some cases it has gone too high and there has been a lack of realisation of the risk/reward balance in these bonds. Going forward people will realise they have gone a bit too far."
"Longer term if the reforms in Latin America continue and the macro-economic numbers continue to look good or get better then there is no reason why the Bradys cannot go up."
